extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for construing method claim limitations to determine whether they are step-plus-function limitations governed by 35 U.S.C. §112, ¶6 (now §112(f)), based on Federal Circuit precedent (Masco v. Mas-Hamilton).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'step[s] for' language signals intent to invoke §112, ¶6
rubrics_metrics.description: In the context of method claims, the use of the term 'steps for' signals the drafter’s intent to invoke §112, ¶6.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal Circuit: 'the use of the term 'steps for' signals the drafter’s intent to invoke §112, ¶6.' Practitioners should treat explicit 'step[s] for' phrasing as a strong indicator that step-plus-function analysis may be appropriate when construing method claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: §112, ¶6 only implicated when steps consist of functions without acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Even where the drafter employs the 'step for' language, §112, ¶6 is implicated only when steps plus function without acts are present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court will apply §112(f) only if the claimed step recites a function and contains no acts — mere 'step for' language alone is not sufficient. Evaluate whether the limitation describes an act (physical deed) versus a pure function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations that recite acts are not step-plus-function limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed step that comprises an act (e.g., 'holding the lever in a position', 'operably connecting the lever and the dial') is not a step-plus-function limitation because it includes an act that precludes §112, ¶6 treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify verbs/phrases that describe concrete actions (holding, connecting, moving, placing, etc.). If the limitation can be construed as an act, do not treat it as a functional-only step under §112(f). The article uses 'holding' and 'operably connecting' as examples of acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations that recite only functions may trigger step-plus-function treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: A limitation phrased as performing a function (e.g., 'transmitting a force') can be a step-plus-function limitation because 'transmitting' is a function rather than an act (per the Court of Claims' characterization).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the limitation contains any descriptive act or only functional language. If only functional language remains and 'step[s] for' is present (or it can be shown there are no acts), then §112(f) may apply. Note: Federal Circuit reversed the Court of Claims on the 'transmitting' step in this case, illustrating factual/contextual uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absent 'step[s] for' language, courts will not apply §112, ¶6 without showing no act exists
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the claim drafter has not signaled intent to invoke §112, ¶6 by using the 'step[s] for' language, the court will not construe a limitation as step-plus-function without a showing that the limitation contains nothing that can be construed as an act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To avoid §112(f) limitation by inference, patentees can avoid 'step(s) for' phrasing and include descriptive acts in method steps. Conversely, challengers seeking §112(f) treatment must demonstrate the absence of any act in the limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation should avoid disrupting patentees' settled expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Circuit referenced Festo to emphasize that decisions should not 'disrupt patentees’ settled expectations regarding the scope of their claims' and therefore construe §112, ¶6 narrowly when not clearly invoked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will be cautious about importing §112(f)-style limitations into claims absent clear indicia (explicit 'step[s] for' or lack of acts). Use of precedent and policy considerations can be invoked to argue for or against applying step-plus-function treatment.
